extracted.intended_audience: stand-up comedians and comedy writers (especially early-career/club performers) interested in comedy craft and avoiding 'hack' material
extracted.subtask_description: A critical guide describing what constitutes 'hack' or low-quality millennial-focused stand-up material and giving evaluative guidance on topics, tropes, and delivery. Aimed at helping performers identify and avoid lazy, overused comedic strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: 1980s-style hack topics (stale clichés)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hack comedians rely on well-worn topics and punchlines that were prevalent in the 1980s (e.g., airplane food, men/women differences, convenience-store clerk stereotypes, fat people eating bacon cheeseburgers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These topics became hack because they were repeatedly used during the comedy boom when clubs paid well. Using these same stock topics today signals laziness and lack of originality. Examples of anti-patterns: 'airplane food' jokes or routine men-vs-women shtick that recycles decades-old premises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regurgitated stock internet lines / meme-joke reliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Using copy-and-pasted, internet-origin stock lines and meme-phrases as punchlines (e.g., 'Party-foul!', 'This is why we can’t have nice things!').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'share if you agree' mentality produces easy, safe jokes that are recognizable but unoriginal. Relying on these memorized, viral one-liners makes material feel recycled and predictable. Anti-pattern: pasting meme-format jokes wholesale onto the stage without transformation or personal spin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Millennial broad generalizations as punchlines
rubrics_metrics.description: Framing millennials with blanket insults or caricatures (e.g., 'Skinny jeans', 'App-Savvy', 'Safe space', 'Everybody gets a trophy', describing degrees as 'useless', or implying all 18–30-year-olds fit a single narrative).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reducing a group to lazy stereotypes is hacky and overused. These sweeping generalizations are easy targets but lack nuance or surprise. If used, they must be made specific, original, or subverted rather than presented as a tired shorthand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lethargic / self-indulgent pizza-and-binge-watching humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes that celebrate laziness, binge-eating, and binge-watching as the core premise ('I watched Netflix until it asked me “are you still watching?”', 'DON’T JUDGE ME, NETFLIX!').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is described as one of comedy’s lowest common denominators: highly relatable but clichéd. These bits work because of broad relatability across age groups, yet they are easy and unambitious. Guidance: such material can succeed only if executed with cleverness, unique perspective, or strong voice (e.g., an astronaut telling jokes about being an astronaut).

rubrics_metrics.name: Taking a safe/agreeable stance on sensitive subjects (pandering)
rubrics_metrics.description: Getting onstage and taking an obviously 'safe' moral or political side to earn applause (e.g., 'Clap if you’re happy the gays can get married').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This produces an easy 'Gimme' applause break and is characteristic of 'social justice hacks'. While a true professional may make even a safe stance land, for many performers this is lazy pandering. Anti-pattern: using obvious moral positions as punchline fodder without craft or risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relying on topical shorthand (hipster/smartphone jokes) as lazy shorthand
rubrics_metrics.description: Using ephemeral cultural markers (e.g., 'hipsters with smartphones', 'app-savvy') as a quick, lazy shorthand for a joke’s premise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Topical shorthand ages quickly and functions like the old airplane-food routine: it tells the audience how to feel instead of surprising them. Because audiences have wide access to comedy, these brief cultural signposts are often already heard and therefore feel stale unless deeply reworked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assuming edginess = quality; avoiding cruel/ignorant viewpoints
rubrics_metrics.description: Belief that 'edgy' material automatically outperforms safe material, contrasted with the warning that articulating cruel or ignorant viewpoints rarely yields laughs and is often unacceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Edginess can be more powerful than pandering, but there is a line: cruel or ignorant takes are unlikely to be funny and can alienate audiences. Good comedic risk involves craft and awareness of audience sensibilities; gratuitous cruelty is an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of originality in the Internet/WiFi era
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the internet exposes audiences to 'all the comedy ever', standards have risen and oversaturation means recycled bits are more likely to fail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performers must bring originality and fresh perspective; relying on clichés or bits easily found online will not satisfy audiences who have broad access to comedic material. This is both a market and artistic imperative in the modern era.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relatability works only with inventive execution
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes about shared everyday experiences (food, TV, laziness) resonate because they reflect common life, but that resonance alone isn't sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relatable material is effective across demographics but must be delivered with originality, specificity, or a surprising angle. The piece notes that many comedians succeed with this formula, but it remains the 'lowest common denominator' unless elevated by craft (example: prefer an astronaut comedian’s unique commute-related set to a generic 'I love pizza' routine).
